articles.title: Curbs on rent rises and holiday lets can offer faster relief for tenants, says EU housing chair
articles.summary: Limits on rent increases and restrictions on holiday rentals can provide quicker relief for households struggling with housing costs, MEP Irene Tinagli said, while warning that lasting solutions require investment in affordable homes.
articles.content:
Limits on rent increases and restrictions on holiday rentals can provide quicker relief for households struggling with housing costs, MEP Irene Tinagli said, while warning that lasting solutions require investment in affordable homes.

Regulation could be the fastest response for tenants facing their next rent payment, Italian MEP Irene Tinagli said. Measures to moderate rent increases and restrict short-term rentals in neighbourhoods under the greatest pressure could help in the short to medium term.

“In the long term we need structural measures that provide a greater supply of affordable homes,” she told the European Newsroom (enr) on Wednesday. That would however require substantial investment and long-term planning, she added.

Tinagli, who chairs the European Parliament’s Special Committee on the Housing Crisis (HOUS), said residential property “has become an asset” and was increasingly attracting investors and real estate funds. These investors were buying entire buildings and evicting tenants or sharply raising rents, she said, describing a pattern seen in cities across the EU.

One such case was Maricarmen Abascal, whose eviction from her longtime Madrid home made her a symbol of Spain’s housing protests. She died in hospital at the age of 87 on October 7, two weeks after her eviction. She never returned home, despite an agreement with the apartment’s owner, Urbagestión, that would have allowed her to return at roughly her previous rent rate.

In the interview, conducted before news of Abascal’s death emerged, Tinagli described Abascal’s eviction as “a case that we are seeing in many other cities and countries across the European Union” and added: “It tells me that we need to do something.”

European tools, local action

While housing remains primarily a national and local responsibility, the EU could provide authorities with tools to act, alongside guidelines and parliamentary resolutions, Tinagli said.

She pointed to greater use of cohesion funds, “reprogramming them to address housing investments”, and more flexible state-aid rules to support social and affordable housing projects.

Work on an Affordable Housing Act, which the European Commission proposed last month, was intended to give authorities clearer criteria for restricting short-term rentals “where they are becoming increasingly invasive of the dynamics of the city,” the Italian politician said.

Such restrictions could range from limits on licences to outright bans, depending on local housing pressures. Reducing potential returns from holiday lets could curb investors’ interest in driving up property prices, she added.
articles.reasoning: The article discusses meaningful policy proposals aimed at protecting tenants from rising rents and evictions, which can improve housing affordability and security for many people across the EU. It highlights both short-term regulatory measures and long-term investments in affordable housing, addressing a widespread social issue with significant public impact.
articles.personality_title: EU plans rent limits and holiday rental rules to help tenants quickly
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many people in European cities are struggling to pay rent because housing prices are rising fast. Investors often buy homes, raise rents, or evict tenants, making it harder for families to stay in their homes.

**What happened** – Irene Tinagli, a member of the European Parliament, said that setting limits on rent increases and restricting short-term holiday rentals can provide faster relief to tenants. She explained that these rules could help neighborhoods under the most pressure. Tinagli also highlighted the need for long-term investment in affordable housing to solve the problem permanently.

**Impact** – This approach is important because it offers immediate help to people facing high rent bills, while also working on bigger solutions. By limiting holiday rentals, cities can stop investors from pushing up prices and evicting tenants. This protects families and keeps communities stable.

**What's next step** – The European Union is working on an Affordable Housing Act to guide local governments on when and how to limit short-term rentals. They also plan to use EU funds and change rules to support building more affordable homes. These actions aim to balance quick relief with lasting improvements in housing.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The EU is combining rent controls and holiday rental limits with plans for affordable homes to help tenants now and in the future.
articles.personality_title_fr: L'UE prévoit des limites sur les loyers et les locations de courte durée pour aider rapidement les locataires
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – De nombreuses personnes dans les villes européennes ont du mal à payer leur loyer car les prix de l'immobilier augmentent rapidement. Les investisseurs achètent souvent des logements, augmentent les loyers ou expulsent les locataires, rendant la situation difficile pour les familles.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Irene Tinagli, membre du Parlement européen, a déclaré que fixer des limites aux augmentations de loyer et restreindre les locations de courte durée pouvaient offrir un soulagement rapide aux locataires. Elle a expliqué que ces règles pourraient aider les quartiers les plus touchés. Tinagli a aussi insisté sur la nécessité d'investir à long terme dans des logements abordables.

**Impact** – Cette approche est importante car elle apporte une aide immédiate aux personnes confrontées à des loyers élevés, tout en travaillant sur des solutions durables. En limitant les locations de vacances, les villes peuvent empêcher les investisseurs de faire monter les prix et d'expulser les locataires, protégeant ainsi les familles.

**Prochaines étapes** – L'Union européenne prépare une loi sur le logement abordable pour guider les autorités locales sur les restrictions à appliquer aux locations de courte durée. Elle prévoit aussi d'utiliser des fonds européens et de modifier des règles pour soutenir la construction de logements abordables. Ces mesures visent à combiner aide rapide et améliorations durables.

**En une phrase** – L'UE associe contrôle des loyers et limites aux locations de vacances à des projets de logements abordables pour aider les locataires aujourd'hui et demain.
articles.personality_title_es: La UE planea límites al alquiler y reglas para alquileres turísticos para ayudar rápido a los inquilinos
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchas personas en ciudades europeas tienen dificultades para pagar el alquiler porque los precios de la vivienda suben rápido. Los inversores suelen comprar casas, subir los alquileres o echar a los inquilinos, dificultando que las familias puedan quedarse en su hogar.

**Qué pasó** – Irene Tinagli, miembro del Parlamento Europeo, dijo que poner límites a las subidas de alquiler y restringir los alquileres turísticos de corta duración puede ofrecer ayuda rápida a los inquilinos. Explicó que estas reglas podrían ayudar a los barrios más afectados. También destacó la necesidad de invertir a largo plazo en viviendas asequibles.

**Impacto** – Este enfoque es importante porque ofrece ayuda inmediata a quienes enfrentan alquileres altos, mientras se trabaja en soluciones duraderas. Al limitar los alquileres turísticos, las ciudades pueden frenar a los inversores que suben precios y expulsan inquilinos, protegiendo a las familias.

**Próximo paso** – La Unión Europea está trabajando en una Ley de Vivienda Asequible para guiar a los gobiernos locales sobre cuándo y cómo limitar los alquileres turísticos. También planean usar fondos de la UE y cambiar reglas para apoyar la construcción de más viviendas asequibles. Estas acciones buscan combinar ayuda rápida con mejoras duraderas.

**Una frase clave** – La UE combina controles de alquiler y límites a los alquileres turísticos con planes de viviendas asequibles para ayudar a los inquilinos ahora y en el futuro.

articles.title: Reform, or lose trust: Governments press the UN to reflect the world as it is
articles.summary: Can the UN still remain relevant if it still looks and acts like the organization it was when it was formed in 1945? The debate over UN reform at the General Assembly in New York last month produced a striking common refrain from a diverse range of Member States.
articles.content:
Many governments believe the United Nations can only remain credible and effective if its institutions better reflect the realities of the 21st century.

From questions of Security Council representation to institutional effectiveness, delegates repeatedly returned to the relationship between power, fairness and legitimacy.

For this third and final analysis piece highlighting key themes, UN News looked at some of the speeches during the annual General Debate of the 193 Member States attending the UN General Assembly.

As Secretary-General António Guterres put it: “The United Nations exists because power requires rules – and humanity needs a place where power answers to principle.”

Who gets a seat at the table?

Security Council reform sat at the centre of discussions about UN reform.

Speaker after speaker argued that representation and legitimacy can't be separated, and Africa's continued absence from permanent membership was a recurrent theme.

UN Photo/Loey Felipe

Kenya put it bluntly: “The equality proclaimed in this Assembly ends at the doors of the Security Council."

Guyana made a similar case for the wider world: “We need a Security Council that reflects the geopolitical realities of the 21st century, not the power structures of 1945; a Council that embraces the emerging multipolarity of our world, including permanent representation from Africa, and Latin America and the Caribbean.”

The UN chief Mr. Guterres agreed, calling the status quo indefensible: “A 21st century Security Council without permanent African seats is unjust and indefensible.”

General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman echoed this sentiment: “Africa cannot be asked to wait indefinitely for its rightful place on the Council.”

UN Photo

Consensus on reform, disagreement over how

While support for reform was widespread, governments proposed different solutions.

Spain went furthest, calling for both fairer regional representation and scrapping the veto outright: “We need to reform the Security Council so that all of the regions in the world have fair representation, and so that we can do away with the right of veto of the permanent members.”

Russia, one of the five Permanent Members of the Council, took a more cautious approach backing “the expansion of representation by Asia, Africa and Latin America” but adding that reforms shouldn't “undermine the intergovernmental nature of the UN system or erode the prerogatives of the UN Security Council and its Permanent Members."

Trust has to be earned

A second thread ran through the week: Trust, and how easily it erodes when rules get applied selectively.

Hungary argued cooperation and self-interest aren't actually in opposition: “We believe that national interest and international cooperation do not have to stand against each other,” adding that “the United Nations cannot demand trust. It must earn it.”

Several delegations linked public confidence in international institutions to the consistent application of rules and principles. Concerns were raised about unequal treatment, selective implementation of international law and failures to respond effectively to crises.

A leaner UN?

While the UN has championed its UN80 Initiative, that aims to make the United Nations more coherent, effective and responsive to today's challenges, countries also offered competing visions of operational reform.

Switzerland and Costa Rica emphasized clear priorities, efficiency and measurable results.

The President of the General Assembly highlighted overlapping mandates, bureaucratic silos and the need for better coordination at the country level.

However, several speakers warned against treating reform as a cost-cutting exercise.

China said reform should improve institutional performance rather than merely reduce budgets and mandates.

Guyana argued that resources should match the responsibilities assigned to the Organization.

Spain called for United Nations agencies, funds and programmes to receive more resources and greater executive capacity.

UN Photo/Yutaka Nagata

The differences were not simply about spending. They concerned what the United Nations should do, how much authority it should have and whether better delivery requires stronger operational capacity – or a narrower institutional role.

Is the UN fit for purpose?

A recurring question throughout the debate was not whether the United Nations should exist, but whether it can produce results.

General Assembly President Rahman put it most sharply: “Outside these walls, people are not asking whether the United Nations still exists. They are asking whether it works.” He maintained that it is people which matter, not process: “Every penny must be invested to achieve impact on the ground for the people we serve.”

The United States offered a contrasting model based on institutional retrenchment: “We cut the UN budget for the first time ever, slashing it by 15 percent in 2026 and eliminating more than 4,000 positions from the UN bureaucracy,” while rejecting international involvement in areas considered national prerogatives.

One line united almost everyone

For all the disagreement over vetoes, institutional power and competing reform models, delegates kept circling back to the same core concern.

Namely that the scale of today's problems has outgrown the structures meant to solve them and that Member States need to work towards building a more resilient and effective organization.

As Guyana noted: “This is why we must not abandon multilateralism because it is imperfect; we must renew it because humanity still needs it.”

This reform effort has broad implications for international cooperation, justice, and global governance, impacting all UN member states and thereby the global community. The article provides detailed context on the debate, key proposals, and the importance of trust and representation, making it a substantive and meaningful story about positive institutional change.
articles.personality_title: UN member states push for reforms to better reflect today’s world
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The United Nations (UN) was created in 1945 to help countries work together and keep peace. But many governments now say the UN’s rules and leadership don’t match the way the world looks today.

**What happened** – In September, leaders from 193 countries met at the UN General Assembly in New York. They talked about changing the UN to make it fairer and more effective. A big topic was the UN Security Council, which has powerful members with permanent seats and veto power. Many said Africa and other regions should have permanent seats too, because the current setup reflects the world of 1945, not 2024. Some countries want to remove the veto power, while others want to keep it but add more members.

**Impact** – These discussions are important because they show a shared belief that the UN must change to stay trusted and useful. When some countries feel left out, it hurts cooperation and trust. The talks also focused on making the UN work better by having clear goals and enough resources. This could help the UN respond faster and more fairly to global problems like conflicts and climate change.

**What’s next step** – The UN will continue these talks to find ways to update its rules and structure. Changing the Security Council is difficult because every permanent member has a veto. But the pressure for reform is growing, and more countries want to see a UN that represents everyone fairly and acts effectively.

**One-sentence takeaway** – UN member states are working together to reform the organization so it better reflects today’s world and earns the trust of all countries.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les États membres de l’ONU poussent à des réformes pour mieux refléter le monde d’aujourd’hui
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – L’Organisation des Nations unies (ONU) a été créée en 1945 pour aider les pays à coopérer et maintenir la paix. Mais de nombreux gouvernements estiment aujourd’hui que les règles et la direction de l’ONU ne correspondent plus à la réalité du monde actuel.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En septembre, les dirigeants de 193 pays se sont réunis à l’Assemblée générale de l’ONU à New York. Ils ont discuté de changements pour rendre l’ONU plus juste et efficace. Un sujet important était le Conseil de sécurité, qui compte des membres permanents puissants avec un droit de veto. Beaucoup ont demandé que l’Afrique et d’autres régions obtiennent des sièges permanents, car la situation actuelle reflète le monde de 1945, pas celui de 2024. Certains pays veulent supprimer le droit de veto, d’autres souhaitent l’élargir tout en le conservant.

**Impact** – Ces discussions sont importantes car elles montrent un consensus : l’ONU doit évoluer pour rester digne de confiance et utile. Quand certains pays se sentent exclus, cela nuit à la coopération et à la confiance. Les débats ont aussi porté sur l’efficacité de l’ONU, avec des objectifs clairs et des ressources suffisantes. Cela pourrait aider l’ONU à mieux répondre aux crises mondiales comme les conflits ou le changement climatique.

**Prochaine étape** – L’ONU poursuivra ces discussions pour trouver des moyens d’actualiser ses règles et sa structure. Modifier le Conseil de sécurité est difficile car chaque membre permanent a un droit de veto. Mais la pression pour une réforme grandit, et de plus en plus de pays veulent une ONU qui représente tous équitablement et agit efficacement.

**En une phrase** – Les États membres de l’ONU travaillent ensemble pour réformer l’organisation afin qu’elle reflète mieux le monde d’aujourd’hui et gagne la confiance de tous les pays.
articles.personality_title_es: Los estados miembros de la ONU impulsan reformas para reflejar mejor el mundo actual
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La Organización de las Naciones Unidas (ONU) se creó en 1945 para ayudar a los países a cooperar y mantener la paz. Pero muchos gobiernos ahora dicen que las reglas y el liderazgo de la ONU no reflejan cómo es el mundo hoy.

**Qué pasó** – En septiembre, líderes de 193 países se reunieron en la Asamblea General de la ONU en Nueva York. Hablaron sobre cambiar la ONU para hacerla más justa y efectiva. Un tema importante fue el Consejo de Seguridad, que tiene miembros permanentes con poder de veto. Muchos dijeron que África y otras regiones deberían tener asientos permanentes porque la estructura actual refleja el mundo de 1945, no el de 2024. Algunos países quieren eliminar el veto, otros quieren mantenerlo y agregar más miembros.

**Impacto** – Estas discusiones son importantes porque muestran que hay un acuerdo en que la ONU debe cambiar para seguir siendo confiable y útil. Cuando algunos países se sienten excluidos, se pierde confianza y cooperación. También se habló de hacer que la ONU funcione mejor, con metas claras y suficientes recursos. Esto podría ayudar a la ONU a responder más rápido y justo a problemas globales como conflictos y cambio climático.

**Próximo paso** – La ONU seguirá hablando para encontrar formas de actualizar sus reglas y estructura. Cambiar el Consejo de Seguridad es difícil porque cada miembro permanente tiene veto. Pero la presión para reformar está creciendo, y más países quieren ver una ONU que represente a todos de manera justa y actúe con eficacia.

**Resumen en una frase** – Los estados miembros de la ONU trabajan juntos para reformar la organización y que refleje mejor el mundo actual ganándose la confianza de todos los países.
